newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Banks' forex profits up, mood sombre.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Banks' forex profits up, mood sombre.

text.p: Banks' foreign exchange profits are swelling in 1997 as currency volatility resurfaces but the mood on the world's biggest market is not altogether upbeat -- and lunches are definitely shorter.
Currency markets, with daily turnover in excess of a trillion dollars, have gone ballistic in 1997.
The U.S. dollar, involved in more than four-fifths of all currency trades, surged to 41-month peaks above 1.74 marks in June, just three days after plummeting to 19-month troughs against the yen.

The mark slumped to near two-year lows against the yen and surged to 1-1/2 year highs against the French franc. And sterling continued its relentless rise this year, soaring to 57-month peaks above 2.84 marks.

"I see increased volatility...And that has led to an improvement in the profits of market-makers generally, throughout the (foreign exchange) market," said Nick Beecroft, head of global spot trading at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Last year, volatility on currency markets shrunk dramatically as convergence in the run-up to European economic and monetary union (EMU), the increase in electronic broking and bank mergers squeezed the life from the foreign exchanges.
The U.S. dollar, for instance, barely moved in 1996 -- trading in a range of no more than eight percent.
With little to do and the mood definitely sombre as layoffs and gloom spread throughout the market, foreign exchange traders spent many hours away from their desks, enjoying long lunches.
WHAT A DIFFERENCE A YEAR MAKES
This year, things have changed.
"People are staying at their desks more than they used to...I would say lunches are definitely shorter than last year," said Duncan Frost from Bank Brussels Lambert's sales desk.

"When you get a day -- like a New York holiday -- with no figures in the afternoon, everybody makes merry. But certainly, lunches are not what they once were," said Peter Wood, trader at Bank of Boston.
With rising currency volatility and improved profits, things are looking up -- for some.
"This year, the mood has changed completely," said DMG's Beecroft.

But currency gyrations could have come in better days. Banks' staffing levels have been pared to the bone after falling revenues in 1996 forced layoffs on many of the traders hired in the dizzy days of 1992 and 1993.

"It is a shrinking market, the development of the electronic broking systems has made quite serious inroads into staffing levels," said Patrick Robinson, associate director at Andersons Recruitment Company.
Despite the pick-up in volatility, the advent of Europe's single currency, planned for 1999, has already sounded a death knell for much of the foreign exchange business.
EMU threatens to wipe out large turnover for trading financial instruments in as many as 15 countries, forcing banks to slash their staffing levels.
"The market had discounted the fact that EMU would take place and over 1995-1996 made manpower adjustments to account for that," said Beecroft.

Ironically, EMU, which thwarted volatility in 1996 as players flocked into convergence trades, based on expectations that European economies will converge in the run-up to monetary union, has caused much of the upheavals in European currencies this year.
"The prime mover for volatility has been Europe. It is becoming so obvious now that even the core European nations won't meet the Maastricht criteria," said BBL's Frost.

French elections, which swept the Socialists into power, and the rift with Germany over the key stability pact also did their bit for currency gyrations, and analysts see the trend likely to continue.
VOLATILE TREND LIKELY TO CONTINUE

"There will be continuing debate about the progress towards EMU and the market will swing between judging the soundness of the euro, on the assumption that EMU does take place, and on the other hand there may be occasions when it will look like EMU could be delayed," said Beecroft.
With staffing levels and expertise shrinking from the once robust European currency sections, a delay to EMU, said analysts, could stretch desks to the limit.
Falling salary levels have also hit traders where it hurts.
"Generally speaking, salaries have come down. And I don't think the bonuses we once saw are out there," said Andersen's Robinson.
For smaller banks, making a fast buck in foreign exchange, where London represents 30 percent of global turnover, has not been easy -- not even with rising volatility.
"There are an awful lot of banks who are not doing as well as they would like to," said Bank of Boston's Wood.
"The big banks still have the big customers, the big flows. But lots of medium-sized to smaller banks who relied on their interbank business are not doing as well," he added.
Many allude to the welcome volatility as a temporary boon.

"Increased volatility has made people more money in the earlier part of this year and it is no secret that it is good for foreign exchange trading. But I don't think it necessarily makes anyone more cheery about loosing half their currencies," said Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase Investment Bank.
